aeo.what_is: Excessive fear or anxiety about separation from attachment figures that's inappropriate for developmental level.

description.overview: Separation Anxiety Disorder (SAD) is characterized by developmentally inappropriate and excessive fear or anxiety concerning separation from those to whom the individual is attached. The anxiety is persistent (lasting at least 4 weeks in children/adolescents and typically 6 months or more in adults) and causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, academic, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The Bedtime Battle
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: Every night, 7-year-old Tyler begs his mom to sleep in his room. He's terrified that if he sleeps alone, something bad will happen to her. He insists she check on him every 15 minutes, and even then, he often ends up in her bed by midnight, unable to bear the distance.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The School Refusal
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: Nina, 9, complains of stomachaches every morning before school. By the time the bus arrives, she's in tears, clinging to her dad and begging not to go. Once at school, she visits the nurse constantly, asking to call home. Her parents are confused—she's always been close to them, but this level of distress is new.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The College Struggle
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: Maya, 18, was excited to start college, but two weeks in, she's calling her mom 10 times a day and coming home every weekend. She can't concentrate in class, imagining car accidents or medical emergencies. Her roommate thinks she's just homesick, but Maya knows it's more—she's terrified something will happen to her family when she's not there.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The New Parent
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: After having her first baby, Sarah, 32, can't leave him for more than an hour without spiraling into panic. She imagines SIDS, accidents, or illness when she's not watching. Her partner offers to babysit so she can have a break, but Sarah refuses—the anxiety of separation is worse than the exhaustion.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The Aging Parent
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: After his father's heart attack, David, 45, calls his elderly parents multiple times a day to check on them. He avoids business trips and cancels evening plans, needing to be nearby 'just in case.' His wife points out his dad is stable now, but David can't shake the fear of losing them when he's not there.

common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that distress is recognized as a real condition, not 'just clinginess'
Confusion about why separation is so much harder than for peers or siblings
Guilt from parents wondering if they were too close or overprotective
Frustration that reassurance doesn't ease the anxiety
Validation that physical symptoms (stomachaches, headaches) are connected to anxiety
Hope that treatment can reduce suffering and improve independence

content.temporal_criteria: Duration of at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents; typically 6 months or more in adults. Must include developmentally inappropriate, excessive fear/anxiety concerning separation from attachment figures.
content.misdiagnosis_explained: Separation anxiety disorder is missed when school refusal or physical complaints are attributed to behavioral problems or medical issues without exploring underlying separation fears. It's over-diagnosed when age-appropriate clinginess in young children (e.g., a 2-year-old crying at daycare drop-off) or culturally normative close family bonds are pathologized without evidence of impairment or excess relative to developmental norms.
content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Developmentally inappropriate, excessive fear/anxiety concerning separation from attachment figures, evidenced by ≥3 symptoms: (1) distress when anticipating/experiencing separation; (2) worry about losing/harm to attachment figures; (3) worry about untoward events causing separation; (4) reluctance/refusal to go out due to separation fear; (5) reluctance/refusal to be alone or without attachment figures; (6) reluctance/refusal to sleep away from home; (7) nightmares about separation; (8) physical complaints when separation occurs/anticipated. B. Duration ≥4 weeks in children/adolescents; typically ≥6 months in adults. C. Causes distress/impairment. D. Not better explained by another mental disorder.
content.prevalence: Estimated 4% in children, 1.6% in adolescents, and ~0.9–1.9% in adults. Slightly more common in females.
content.age_of_onset: Most common onset in childhood (7–9 years), but can emerge in adolescence or adulthood, often after a stressor such as illness, relocation, or relationship loss.
content.prognosis: Often remits with treatment, especially in childhood, but may persist into adulthood if untreated. Comorbid anxiety or mood disorders can complicate recovery.
content.neurobiology: Separation Anxiety Disorder involves dysregulation of neural circuits mediating attachment, threat detection, and emotional regulation. Functional imaging studies suggest heightened amygdala activation in response to separation cues and altered connectivity with prefrontal regions, potentially leading to exaggerated fear responses. Dysfunctions in the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis have been noted, with atypical cortisol responses to stress. The disorder may share genetic and neurobiological vulnerabilities with other anxiety disorders, including serotonin transporter gene variations and heightened autonomic arousal during separation-related stress.

history_psychosocial: Nature, onset, and duration of separation fears.
Situations avoided, functional impairment, and associated somatic symptoms.
medical_assessment: Rule out medical causes for physical complaints during separation (e.g., GI upset, headaches).
standardized_measures: Screen for Child Anxiety Related Emotional Disorders (SCARED)
Revised Children's Anxiety and Depression Scale (RCADS)

emotional_cognitive: Excessive worry about harm to attachment figures
Fear of being alone or without attachment figures
behavioral: School refusal or reluctance to leave home
physical: Headaches, stomachaches, nausea, or other somatic symptoms when separation is anticipated or occurs

severity_levels.mild: Anxiety manageable with coping strategies; mild avoidance and impairment.
severity_levels.moderate: Frequent anxiety and avoidance significantly impacting school/work and relationships.
severity_levels.severe: Persistent, intense anxiety with marked functional impairment and distress.

biological: Family history of anxiety or mood disorders

impact_on_life.school_work: Absenteeism, academic decline, difficulty participating in group activities.
impact_on_life.social: Reduced peer interactions, avoidance of overnight stays or travel.
impact_on_life.emotional: Persistent distress, worry, and possible depressive symptoms.

psychotherapy: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) — gradual exposure to separation, cognitive restructuring.
Parent-based interventions to reduce accommodation of anxiety behaviors.
Family therapy to address attachment dynamics.
school_interventions: Collaboration with school for graded re-entry, predictable routines, and support strategies.
medications: SSRIs considered for severe or refractory cases, especially with comorbid anxiety/depression.

treatment_goals: Support consistent school attendance and peer engagement.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Attributing school refusal solely to behavioral problems without exploring anxiety.
Overlooking separation anxiety in adolescents or adults.
overdiagnosis_factors: Pathologizing age-appropriate clinginess in young children.
Misinterpreting cultural norms favoring close family bonds.
warning_signs: Prolonged distress during separations beyond developmental norms.
Physical symptoms consistently occurring before or during separations.
Avoidance of essential activities due to separation fears.
self_help_strategies: Gradually increase time spent apart in a supportive way.
Use coping skills such as relaxation or grounding before separations.

first_person_statements: I knew it was irrational to think something would happen to my mom if I went to school, but the fear was so overwhelming I couldn't function.
People thought I was just clingy, but I was genuinely terrified every time I had to leave my parents.
Therapy helped me learn that separations don't mean disaster—I could tolerate the discomfort without catastrophe.
As an adult, I finally recognized that my need to constantly check in with my partner was separation anxiety, not love.
The stomachaches before school were real, even though the doctors said nothing was wrong. It was my anxiety talking.
Learning to tolerate being apart was like facing my biggest fear every day—but it got easier with practice.

real_life_examples.title: The Elementary Escape Artist
real_life_examples.story: At 8, Jordan began refusing to go to school. Every morning was a battle—crying, pleading, physical resistance. His parents tried rewards, consequences, and reassurance, but nothing worked. His pediatrician found no medical cause for Jordan's frequent stomachaches. Finally, a child psychologist uncovered the root: Jordan was terrified something would happen to his mother while he was at school. His anxiety had started after his grandmother died unexpectedly; now Jordan couldn't bear to be separated from his mom. Treatment involved gradual exposure—starting with short separations at home, then brief school visits with mom nearby, building to full days. His therapist also worked with Jordan on cognitive restructuring, helping him see that his worry wasn't keeping his mom safe. His parents learned to resist reassuring him repeatedly, which only fed the anxiety loop. Over several months, Jordan's attendance improved. Mornings were still hard sometimes, but he learned he could tolerate the discomfort and that his fears didn't come true.

real_life_examples.title: The College Comeback
real_life_examples.story: Maya had been excited to start college across the country, but two weeks in, she was in crisis. She called her parents constantly, convinced something terrible would happen to them or her younger brother. She couldn't focus in class, skipped social events, and came home every weekend. Her roommate thought it was homesickness, but Maya knew it was more. She'd always been close to her family, but this level of panic was new. A campus counselor diagnosed separation anxiety disorder and explained that the transition to college—combined with her anxious temperament—had triggered it. Through CBT, Maya learned to challenge her catastrophic thoughts and tolerate uncertainty. She practiced staying on campus for longer stretches, using grounding techniques when anxiety spiked. Her parents learned to limit phone calls to scheduled times and resist giving constant reassurance. By sophomore year, Maya had found her footing—she still missed her family, but the paralyzing fear had eased, and she could enjoy her independence.

real_life_examples.title: The Adult Realization
real_life_examples.story: At 38, Mark finally understood why he'd always struggled with his wife's business trips. He'd tell himself he was just 'missing her,' but the truth was darker: he imagined plane crashes, car accidents, hotel fires. He'd check flight trackers obsessively and text her constantly. After she left for a week-long conference and Mark spent the entire time in a state of low-grade panic, barely sleeping and unable to work, he sought help. His therapist diagnosed separation anxiety disorder—Mark was shocked to learn it could affect adults. Therapy revealed that Mark's father had died suddenly when Mark was 10, leaving a deep fear of losing loved ones. Through CBT and EMDR to process the trauma, Mark learned to tolerate his wife's absences without catastrophizing. He practiced mindfulness and challenged his anxious thoughts with evidence. It wasn't easy, but over time, Mark could say goodbye without spiraling into dread.

comparisons.explanation: Separation anxiety disorder is specifically focused on fear of separation from attachment figures (parents, partners, children). GAD involves chronic, excessive worry about multiple life domains (health, work, finances, relationships) without a primary focus on separation. Someone with separation anxiety might worry only when apart from loved ones, while someone with GAD worries broadly and persistently about many things.

Separation anxiety centers on fear of being apart from attachment figures and worry about harm coming to them. Social anxiety centers on fear of judgment, embarrassment, or humiliation in social situations. While both can lead to avoidance (school refusal, for example), the underlying fear is different: separation anxiety is about losing or being apart from loved ones, while social anxiety is about being negatively evaluated by others.

Panic disorder with agoraphobia involves fear of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable if a panic attack occurs, leading to avoidance of places like crowded stores or public transport. Separation anxiety disorder involves fear of being away from specific attachment figures. While both can cause avoidance of leaving home, the motivation differs: agoraphobia is about fear of panic symptoms in certain places, while separation anxiety is about fear of harm to or distance from loved ones.

faqs.question: Isn't some separation anxiety normal in young children?
faqs.answer: Yes, separation anxiety is a normal developmental phase, typically peaking between 8–14 months and again around 2–3 years. It becomes a disorder when it's excessive for the child's age, persists for at least 4 weeks, and causes significant distress or impairment (like consistent school refusal or inability to sleep alone well past the age when peers can).

faqs.question: Can adults have separation anxiety disorder?
faqs.answer: Yes. Adults can develop separation anxiety, often triggered by life stressors like illness, loss of a loved one, or major transitions. Adult separation anxiety often manifests as excessive worry about romantic partners or children, difficulty being apart, and avoidance of travel or work opportunities that require separation.

faqs.question: Why does separation anxiety cause physical symptoms like stomachaches?
faqs.answer: Anxiety activates the body's stress response, which affects the digestive system, heart rate, and other physical functions. For children especially, who may not yet have the vocabulary to express emotional distress, anxiety often manifests as physical complaints. The stomachaches are real, even if there's no medical illness causing them.

faqs.question: How is separation anxiety disorder different from attachment issues?
faqs.answer: Attachment issues (like insecure or disorganized attachment) describe the quality of the bond between a child and caregiver, often rooted in early caregiving experiences. Separation anxiety disorder is an anxiety disorder characterized by excessive fear of separation. They can overlap—insecure attachment is a risk factor for separation anxiety—but they're distinct concepts. You can have secure attachment and still develop separation anxiety disorder after a stressor.

faqs.question: Will my child's separation anxiety get worse if I accommodate it?
faqs.answer: Accommodation (like letting a child sleep in your bed every night or staying home from work to ease their anxiety) provides short-term relief but often reinforces the anxiety long-term. It sends the message that separations are dangerous and the child can't cope. Treatment involves gradually reducing accommodation while teaching the child coping skills and building tolerance for separation.

faqs.question: Can separation anxiety disorder be cured?
faqs.answer: Many children and adults achieve full remission with treatment, especially with early intervention. Some individuals may always have a tendency toward separation concerns but learn to manage them effectively so they don't interfere with life. The goal is not to eliminate all separation distress but to reduce it to a manageable, age-appropriate level.

faqs.question: How do I help my child with separation anxiety disorder?
faqs.answer: Seek professional help from a therapist who specializes in childhood anxiety. At home, maintain consistent routines, practice brief separations with predictable reunions, resist excessive reassurance, validate feelings without reinforcing avoidance, and model calm goodbyes. Collaborate closely with your child's school and therapist for a coordinated approach.

faqs.question: Is medication necessary for separation anxiety disorder?
faqs.answer: Not always. Therapy (especially CBT with exposure) is the first-line treatment. Medication (like SSRIs) may be considered for severe cases, when therapy alone isn't sufficient, or when there's comorbid depression or another anxiety disorder. Many children respond well to therapy without medication.

faqs.question: Can separation anxiety disorder develop after a traumatic event?
faqs.answer: Yes. Life stressors like a parent's illness, death of a family member, natural disaster, or relocation can trigger separation anxiety disorder, especially in individuals with anxious temperaments or family histories of anxiety. Treatment often involves addressing the trauma alongside the separation fears.

faqs.question: What's the difference between separation anxiety disorder and school refusal?
faqs.answer: School refusal is a behavior (refusing to attend school) that can have many causes, including separation anxiety disorder, social anxiety, bullying, learning difficulties, or depression. Separation anxiety disorder is a specific diagnosis involving excessive fear of separation from attachment figures. Not all school refusal is due to separation anxiety, and separation anxiety can exist without school refusal.

faqs.question: Separation anxiety disorder vs. GAD—what's the difference?
faqs.answer: Separation anxiety disorder is focused specifically on fear of separation from attachment figures and worry about harm coming to them. GAD involves chronic, excessive worry spanning multiple domains (health, work, finances, relationships, world events) with no single focus. Someone with separation anxiety worries primarily when apart from loved ones; someone with GAD worries broadly about many things.

faqs.question: How is separation anxiety disorder different from social anxiety disorder?
faqs.answer: Separation anxiety is about fear of being apart from specific people and worry about harm to them. Social anxiety is about fear of judgment, embarrassment, or humiliation in social or performance situations. Both can cause school refusal, but the reasons differ: separation anxiety involves fear of leaving home or parents, while social anxiety involves fear of being scrutinized by peers or teachers.

faqs.question: Separation anxiety disorder vs. panic disorder with agoraphobia—what's the distinction?
faqs.answer: Panic disorder with agoraphobia involves fear of places or situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable if panic symptoms occur, leading to avoidance of public spaces. Separation anxiety involves fear of being away from attachment figures and worry about harm to them. Both can lead to staying home, but panic/agoraphobia is about fear of panic symptoms in certain locations, while separation anxiety is about distance from loved ones.

faqs.question: Can separation anxiety disorder run in families?
faqs.answer: Yes, there's a genetic component—separation anxiety and other anxiety disorders tend to run in families. If a parent has an anxiety disorder, children are at higher risk. However, environment also plays a role: overprotective parenting, family stress, or modeling anxious behaviors can contribute.

faqs.question: How long does treatment take?
faqs.answer: It varies. Some children show improvement within a few months of CBT, while others need longer. Consistency is key—regular therapy sessions, home practice of skills, and collaboration with schools. Adults may take longer due to more entrenched patterns. Expect gradual progress, not overnight change.

faqs.question: What if my child's separation anxiety disorder doesn't improve?
faqs.answer: If there's no progress after several months of consistent therapy, reassess with your provider. Consider whether there are complicating factors (trauma, family stress, undiagnosed conditions), whether accommodations at home are reinforcing anxiety, or whether medication might help. Sometimes a different therapeutic approach or therapist is needed.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek professional help if fear of separation is persistent, excessive for developmental level, and interferes with school, work, or relationships.
